title: Entropy increases with dispersal of matter
body: Entropy increases when matter becomes more dispersed: solid to liquid to gas, a gas expanding into a larger volume at constant T, or more moles of gas in the products than in the reactants.
caution: Justify an entropy sign with the specific particles (e.g., gas moles produced or consumed, particles freer to move in a larger volume). Vague 'more order/less disorder' wording alone does not earn credit.
ced_evidence: 9.1.A.1 "Entropy increases when matter becomes more dispersed"

title: Entropy increases with temperature (energy dispersal)
body: Entropy increases when energy is dispersed: the distribution of kinetic energy among gas particles broadens as temperature rises, so the entropy of the system increases with temperature.
ced_evidence: 9.1.A.2 "the distribution of kinetic energy among the particles of a gas broadens as the temperature increases"

title: Standard entropy change of a reaction
body: \Delta S^{\circ}_{reaction}=\Sigma S^{\circ}_{products}-\Sigma S^{\circ}_{reactants}
ced_evidence: 9.2.A.1 EQN: ΔS°reaction = ΣS°products − ΣS°reactants

title: Thermodynamically favored
body: A process is thermodynamically favored when its standard Gibbs free energy change is negative (ΔG° < 0); this term is preferred over 'spontaneous', which is often misread as 'suddenly' or 'without cause'.
caution: Use 'thermodynamically favored' rather than 'spontaneous'; favored does not mean fast.
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.2 "When ΔGo < 0 for the process, it is said to be thermodynamically favored."

title: Standard state (for ΔG°)
body: ΔG° applies when all reactants and products are in a standard state: pure substances, solutions of 1.0 M concentration, or gases at 1.0 atm (or 1.0 bar).
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.1 "as pure substances, as solutions of 1.0 M concentration, or as gases at a pressure of 1.0 atm (or 1.0 bar)"

title: ΔG° from standard free energies of formation
body: \Delta G^{\circ}_{reaction}=\Sigma\Delta G_f^{\circ}{}_{products}-\Sigma\Delta G_f^{\circ}{}_{reactants}
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.3 EQN: ΔG°reaction = ΣΔGf°products − ΣΔGf°reactants

title: Gibbs free energy equation
body: \Delta G^{\circ}=\Delta H^{\circ}-T\Delta S^{\circ}
caution: When explaining favorability, state which term (enthalpy or entropy) actually has the sign supporting ΔG° < 0; do not claim both contribute favorably unless both do.
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.5 EQN: ΔG° = ΔH° − T ΔS°

title: Signs of ΔH° and ΔS° and temperatures favoring ΔG° < 0
body: The signs of ΔH° and ΔS° predict the temperatures at which a process is thermodynamically favored.

items.label: ΔH° < 0, ΔS° > 0
items.meaning: Favored at all T; no calculation needed to show ΔG° < 0

items.label: ΔH° > 0, ΔS° < 0
items.meaning: Favored at no T; no calculation needed to show ΔG° > 0

ced_evidence: 9.3.A.6 "temperature conditions for a process to be thermodynamically favored (ΔG° < 0) can be predicted from the signs of ΔH° and ΔS°"

title: Kinetic control
body: A process that is thermodynamically favored but does not proceed at a measurable rate is under kinetic control, commonly because of high activation energy.
caution: A lack of observable reaction does not mean the system is at equilibrium.
ced_evidence: 9.4.A.2 "Processes that are thermodynamically favored, but do not proceed at a measurable rate, are under 'kinetic control.'"

title: Equilibrium constant from ΔG°
body: K=e^{-\Delta G^{\circ}/RT}
ced_evidence: 9.5.A.2 EQN: K = e^(−ΔG°/RT)

title: ΔG° from the equilibrium constant
body: \Delta G^{\circ}=-RT\ln K
ced_evidence: 9.5.A.2 EQN: ΔG° = −RT ln K

title: Sign of ΔG° and size of K
body: ΔG° < 0 means K > 1 (products favored at equilibrium); ΔG° > 0 means K < 1 (reactants favored); ΔG° near zero means K is close to 1, and K deviates strongly from 1 when |ΔG°| is much larger than RT.
ced_evidence: 9.5.A.3-4 "Processes with ΔG° < 0 favor products (i.e., K > 1)"

title: Factors in the free energy of dissolution
body: ΔG° of dissolution reflects three factors, each with enthalpic and entropic contributions whose signs and relative magnitudes can be estimated; the total is hard to predict because they largely cancel.

items.meaning: Breaking the intermolecular interactions that hold the solid together
Reorganization of the solvent around the dissolved species
Interaction of the dissolved species with the solvent

ced_evidence: 9.6.A.1 "the breaking of the intermolecular interactions that hold the solid together, the reorganization of the solvent..."

title: Driving an unfavorable process with external energy
body: An external energy source (electrical energy for an electrolytic cell or battery charging, light for photosynthesis) can make a thermodynamically unfavorable process occur.
ced_evidence: 9.7.A.1 "An external source of energy can be used to make a thermodynamically unfavorable process occur."

title: Coupled reactions
body: An unfavorable reaction that makes a desired product is coupled to a favorable reaction (e.g., ATP to ADP) through one or more shared common intermediates, and the summed overall reaction has ΔG° < 0.
ced_evidence: 9.7.A.2 "the individual reactions share one or more common intermediates"

title: Oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode
body: In all electrochemical cells, galvanic and electrolytic, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction occurs at the cathode.
caution: Do not assume the anode/cathode role from an earlier part of a question carries over; reassign it from which half-reaction is oxidation and which is reduction in each new cell.
ced_evidence: 9.8.A.3 "oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction occurs at the cathode"

hooks.when_to_use: When assigning which electrode hosts oxidation and which hosts reduction.
hooks.caution: In the answer, state in words that oxidation (loss of electrons) occurs at the anode and reduction (gain of electrons) at the cathode; do not write the mnemonic as the justification.

title: Galvanic vs. electrolytic cells
body: Galvanic (voltaic) cells involve a thermodynamically favored reaction, whereas electrolytic cells involve a thermodynamically unfavored reaction that needs an applied potential.
ced_evidence: 9.8.A.2 "Galvanic, sometimes called voltaic, cells involve a thermodynamically favored reaction, whereas electrolytic cells involve a thermodynamically unfavored reaction."

title: Electrochemical cell diagram
body: Cell diagrams are read to identify where each half-reaction occurs, the direction of current and electron flow, and the cell type; each component has a specific role.

items.label: Electrodes
items.meaning: Anode (oxidation) and cathode (reduction); mass change or gas evolution can occur at an electrode

items.label: Half-cell solutions
items.meaning: Contain the active species of each half-reaction

ced_evidence: 9.8.A.1 "electrodes, solutions in the half-cells, salt bridge, voltage/current measuring device"

title: Standard cell potential from half-reactions
body: Identify the oxidation and reduction half-reactions and use their standard reduction potentials to calculate the standard cell potential E°; a positive E° means the reaction is thermodynamically favored and a negative E° means it is unfavored.
caution: To find the maximum cell potential, pick the pairing in which the oxidation and reduction roles give the largest positive E°; a metal's role can change from one part of a question to the next.
ced_evidence: 9.9.A.2 "identifying the oxidation and reduction half-reactions and their respective standard reduction potentials"

title: Free energy and standard cell potential
body: \Delta G^{\circ}=-nFE^{\circ}
ced_evidence: 9.9.A.3 EQN: ΔGo = −nFEo

title: Nernst equation (qualitative use)
body: E=E^{\circ}-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q
caution: A bare numeric Nernst calculation is not enough; add a qualitative justification of how concentration or Q changes the cell potential relative to E°.
ced_evidence: 9.10.A.4 "the qualitative use of the Nernst equation: E = Eo − (RT/nF) ln Q"

title: Cell potential and distance from equilibrium
body: Standard conditions have Q = 1; moving farther from equilibrium than Q = 1 increases |E| relative to E°, moving closer decreases it, and E = 0 at equilibrium (Q = K).
caution: Le Châtelier's principle does not apply to electrochemical cells because they are not at equilibrium; justify with distance from equilibrium and Q versus K instead.
ced_evidence: 9.10.A.3 "reaching zero at equilibrium (when Q = K)"; 9.10.A.2

title: Current and charge
body: I=\frac{q}{t}
ced_evidence: 9.11.A.1 EQN: I = q/t

title: Quantities related by Faraday's laws
body: Faraday's laws relate these quantities in the stoichiometry of a redox reaction in an electrochemical cell.

items.label: ii
items.meaning: Mass of material deposited on or removed from an electrode (as in electroplating)

ced_evidence: 9.11.A.1 "Faraday's laws can be used to determine the stoichiometry of the redox reaction"
